top_categories.workout_context: Road-specific control matters at Tour of the Battenkill — Gran Fondo. Practice on mixed-surface — paved roads and packed dirt farm: use smooth gear and cadence changes, accelerate deliberately out of corners, and settle quickly back into sustainable power for 64 miles.
Race-pace efforts that mimic Tour of the Battenkill — Gran Fondo's demands. Pacing, fueling, and tactical decisions under fatigue. Practice the race before May.
70ft/mi signals a climbing-heavy course. Sustained sub-threshold and threshold work builds the steady power needed without turning the opening climb into the day’s hardest effort.
When someone attacks on mixed-surface — paved roads and packed dirt farm, you have 10 seconds to respond or you're off the back. This builds that response.

Brief efforts above sustainable power can come from grade changes, positioning, or closing a gap at Tour of the Battenkill — Gran Fondo. Train them without letting those efforts derail the longer pacing plan.
At Tour of the Battenkill — Gran Fondo, changes in grade or pace can lift effort above threshold before it settles again. Over-unders train that transition while you keep riding.
88–92% FTP is where you'll spend the hardest sustained miles of Tour of the Battenkill — Gran Fondo. Train it until it feels boring.

Steeper ramps, positioning, or pace changes on mixed-surface — paved roads and packed dirt farm can demand short hard efforts. Practice them without compromising the sustained work that defines the course.
64 miles on mixed-surface — paved roads and packed dirt farm burns energy faster than the distance suggests. Train the fade resistance now.
Varied gradients on mixed-surface — paved roads and packed dirt farm demand climbing versatility. Sit the shallow stuff, stand the steep stuff, switch without thinking.
Smooth pedaling at 64 miles saves muscle. Bad technique at mile 10 is invisible. At mile 80 it's a cramp.
Double-threshold training builds sustained power with less fatigue. More FTP per hour of training.
